blocks.body:
The zeta function begins as a simple series, $\sum n^{-s}$, and becomes the central object of analytic number theory. Its Euler product ties it to the primes; its continuation and special values tie it to Bernoulli numbers and to $\pi$; and the positions of its zeros control the error term in the prime number theorem.

This lesson builds the basic facts: the continuation past the line $\operatorname{Re} s = 1$, the simple pole at $s = 1$, Euler's evaluation of $\zeta(2k)$, the values at the negative integers, and the first facts about zeros. Euler found $\zeta(2) = \pi^2/6$ in 1735; Riemann's paper of 1859 made $\zeta$ a function of a complex variable and showed why its zeros matter.

blocks.title: The Riemann zeta function
blocks.body:
For complex $s$ with $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$,
$$\zeta(s) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{1}{n^s} = \prod_p\frac{1}{1 - p^{-s}}.$$
The series and the product converge absolutely there ([[dirichlet-series]]), so $\zeta$ is holomorphic and nonzero in this half-plane. For other $s$, $\zeta(s)$ means the analytic continuation constructed below.

blocks.title: Crossing the line Re s = 1
blocks.body:
The series diverges at every $s$ with $\operatorname{Re} s \le 1$: for $\operatorname{Re} s \le 0$ its terms do not even tend to $0$, and for $0 < \operatorname{Re} s \le 1$ its partial sums $\sum_{n\le N}n^{-s}$ behave like $N^{1-s}/(1-s)$ plus a constant (like $\log N$ when $s = 1$) and do not converge. To go further we need another formula for the same function. Here is the simplest. For $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$,
$$s\int_1^\infty\lfloor x\rfloor\,x^{-s-1}\,dx = \sum_{n\ge1}s\int_n^\infty x^{-s-1}\,dx = \sum_{n\ge1}n^{-s} = \zeta(s),$$
because $\lfloor x\rfloor = \sum_{n\le x}1$ and the swap of sum and integral is justified by absolute convergence. Now write $\lfloor x\rfloor = x - \{x\}$, with $\{x\} \in [0,1)$ the fractional part. The $x$ part gives $s\int_1^\infty x^{-s}\,dx = \frac{s}{s-1}$, so
$$\zeta(s) = \frac{s}{s-1} - s\int_1^\infty\{x\}\,x^{-s-1}\,dx.$$
The last integral converges absolutely for $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$, since $|\{x\}x^{-s-1}| \le x^{-\operatorname{Re}s-1}$, and it is holomorphic there. So the right side is the [[continuation|analytic continuation]] of $\zeta$ to $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$, and its only singularity is a simple pole at $s = 1$ with residue $1$.

Near $s = 1$, $\frac{s}{s-1} = 1 + \frac{1}{s-1}$, so
$$\zeta(s) = \frac{1}{s-1} + \gamma + O(s-1), \qquad \gamma = 1 - \int_1^\infty\frac{\{x\}}{x^2}\,dx = 0.5772\ldots,$$
which is Euler's constant (Exercise 2 identifies it with $\lim_N(\sum_{n\le N}1/n - \log N)$).

The same formula gives bounds for real $s > 1$. Since $0 \le \{x\} < 1$, the subtracted term lies strictly between $0$ and $s\int_1^\infty x^{-s-1}\,dx = 1$, so
$$\frac{1}{s-1} < \zeta(s) < \frac{s}{s-1}.$$
In particular $\zeta(s) \sim 1/(s-1)$ as $s \to 1^+$.

blocks.title: Continuation to the whole plane
blocks.body: $\zeta$ extends to a meromorphic function on $\mathbb C$ whose only pole is a simple pole at $s = 1$ with residue $1$.

blocks.title: About the proof
blocks.body: Two proofs are standard. Repeating the integration by parts above with more terms of the Euler–Maclaurin formula ([[partial-summation]]) extends the formula to $\operatorname{Re} s > -k$ for any $k$. Riemann's own proof, through the theta function and Poisson summation, gives at the same time the functional equation relating $\zeta(s)$ and $\zeta(1-s)$, in which the [[gamma|gamma function]] appears; it is the subject of [[functional-equation]]. We use the theorem here and refer there for the proof.

blocks.title: Bernoulli numbers
blocks.body:
The even values involve the Bernoulli numbers, defined by the power series
$$\frac{t}{e^t - 1} = \sum_{n\ge0}B_n\frac{t^n}{n!} \qquad (|t| < 2\pi).$$
The first ones are $B_0 = 1$, $B_1 = -\tfrac12$, $B_2 = \tfrac16$, $B_4 = -\tfrac{1}{30}$, $B_6 = \tfrac{1}{42}$, $B_8 = -\tfrac{1}{30}$, $B_{10} = \tfrac{5}{66}$, $B_{12} = -\tfrac{691}{2730}$, and $B_n = 0$ for every odd $n \ge 3$. The last fact holds because
$$\frac{t}{e^t-1} + \frac t2 = \frac t2\cdot\frac{e^t+1}{e^t-1} = \frac t2\coth\frac t2$$
is an even function of $t$.

blocks.title: Euler's formula for ζ(2k)
blocks.body:
For every integer $k \ge 1$,
$$\zeta(2k) = \frac{(-1)^{k+1}B_{2k}(2\pi)^{2k}}{2\,(2k)!}.$$
So $\zeta(2) = \frac{\pi^2}{6}$, $\zeta(4) = \frac{\pi^4}{90}$, $\zeta(6) = \frac{\pi^6}{945}$, and every $\zeta(2k)$ is a rational multiple of $\pi^{2k}$.

We use the partial-fraction expansion of the cotangent,
$$\pi z\cot\pi z = 1 - 2\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{z^2}{n^2 - z^2} \qquad (z \notin \mathbb Z).$$
It comes from Example 2 of [[fourier-poisson]], which proves $\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}(n^2+a^2)^{-1} = \frac{\pi}{a}\coth\pi a$ for $a > 0$. Both sides are meromorphic in $a$, so the identity persists for complex $a$, and putting $a = iz$ (with $\coth(i\pi z) = -i\cot\pi z$) gives the expansion above.

For $|z| < 1$ expand each term as a geometric series, $\frac{z^2}{n^2 - z^2} = \sum_{k\ge1}(z/n)^{2k}$, and sum over $n$ first (everything converges absolutely):
$$\pi z\cot\pi z = 1 - 2\sum_{k\ge1}\zeta(2k)\,z^{2k}.$$
On the other hand, $\cot\pi z = i\,\frac{e^{2\pi iz}+1}{e^{2\pi iz}-1}$, so with $t = 2\pi iz$,
$$\pi z\cot\pi z = \frac t2\cdot\frac{e^t+1}{e^t-1} = \frac t2\coth\frac t2 = \sum_{k\ge0}B_{2k}\frac{t^{2k}}{(2k)!} = \sum_{k\ge0}\frac{(-1)^kB_{2k}(2\pi)^{2k}}{(2k)!}z^{2k}.$$
Comparing coefficients of $z^{2k}$ for $k \ge 1$ gives $-2\zeta(2k) = (-1)^kB_{2k}(2\pi)^{2k}/(2k)!$, which is the formula.

blocks.title: Values at the negative integers
blocks.body:
Euler also found, by daring manipulations of divergent series, the values of $\zeta$ at the negative integers. In modern form they are values of the continuation:
$$\zeta(0) = -\frac12, \qquad \zeta(-n) = -\frac{B_{n+1}}{n+1}\quad (n \ge 1).$$
Thus $\zeta(-1) = -\tfrac{1}{12}$, $\zeta(-3) = \tfrac{1}{120}$, $\zeta(-5) = -\tfrac{1}{252}$, and $\zeta(-2) = \zeta(-4) = \cdots = 0$ because the odd Bernoulli numbers vanish. These are the trivial zeros. The formula with $B_{n+1}$ also covers $n = 0$ if one uses the convention $B_1 = +\tfrac12$; with the convention $B_1 = -\tfrac12$ used here, $\zeta(0) = -\tfrac12$ must be stated separately. All of these values follow from $\zeta(2k)$ and the functional equation, as shown in [[functional-equation]].

blocks.title: Zeros
blocks.body:
By the Euler product, $\zeta(s) \ne 0$ for $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$. In 1896 Hadamard and de la Vallée Poussin independently proved that $\zeta(1+it) \ne 0$ for every real $t$, which is the key step in the [[pnt|prime number theorem]]. Combined with the functional equation, this shows that apart from the trivial zeros, every zero of $\zeta$ lies in the critical strip $0 < \operatorname{Re} s < 1$. These are the nontrivial zeros. Since $\zeta(\bar s) = \overline{\zeta(s)}$, they are symmetric about the real axis, and the functional equation makes them symmetric about the line $\operatorname{Re} s = \tfrac12$ as well. The first three, in the upper half-plane, are approximately
$$\tfrac12 + 14.1347i, \qquad \tfrac12 + 21.0220i, \qquad \tfrac12 + 25.0109i.$$
The [[rh|Riemann hypothesis]] asserts that every nontrivial zero has real part $\tfrac12$. Riemann's 1859 paper showed how these zeros govern the distribution of primes; the precise statement is the [[explicit-formula]].

blocks.title: The next even values
blocks.solution:
For $k = 2$: $\zeta(4) = \dfrac{(-1)^3B_4(2\pi)^4}{2\cdot 4!} = \dfrac{\tfrac{1}{30}\cdot16\pi^4}{48} = \dfrac{16\pi^4}{1440} = \dfrac{\pi^4}{90}$.

For $k = 3$: $\zeta(6) = \dfrac{(-1)^4B_6(2\pi)^6}{2\cdot 6!} = \dfrac{\tfrac{1}{42}\cdot64\pi^6}{1440} = \dfrac{64\pi^6}{60480} = \dfrac{\pi^6}{945}$.

Numerically $\pi^4/90 = 1.08232\ldots$ and $\pi^6/945 = 1.01734\ldots$, in agreement with the series: the terms beyond $n = 1$ contribute only about $0.08$ and $0.017$.

blocks.title: Sums of zeta values
blocks.solution:
For $k \ge 2$, $\zeta(k) - 1 = \sum_{m\ge2}m^{-k}$. All terms are positive, so the double sum may be rearranged freely:
$$\sum_{k\ge2}\sum_{m\ge2}\frac{1}{m^k} = \sum_{m\ge2}\frac{m^{-2}}{1 - m^{-1}} = \sum_{m\ge2}\frac{1}{m(m-1)} = \sum_{m\ge2}\Bigl(\frac{1}{m-1} - \frac1m\Bigr) = 1.$$
For the even values,
$$\sum_{k\ge1}\sum_{m\ge2}\frac{1}{m^{2k}} = \sum_{m\ge2}\frac{1}{m^2 - 1} = \frac12\sum_{m\ge2}\Bigl(\frac{1}{m-1} - \frac{1}{m+1}\Bigr) = \frac12\Bigl(1 + \frac12\Bigr) = \frac34.$$
Subtracting, $\sum_{k\ge1}(\zeta(2k+1) - 1) = \tfrac14$: the odd values, for which no closed form is known, still have an exact sum.

blocks.title: Coprime pairs
blocks.body: Choose integers $a, b$ independently and uniformly from $\{1, \dots, N\}$. Show that the probability that $\gcd(a,b) = 1$ tends to $1/\zeta(2) = 6/\pi^2$ as $N \to \infty$.
blocks.solution:
By Möbius inversion ([[mobius]]), $\sum_{d\mid g}\mu(d)$ is $1$ if $g = 1$ and $0$ otherwise. Apply it with $g = \gcd(a,b)$; the divisors of $\gcd(a,b)$ are the common divisors of $a$ and $b$. Swapping the order of summation, the number of coprime pairs is
$$C(N) = \sum_{a,b\le N}\ \sum_{d\mid a,\ d\mid b}\mu(d) = \sum_{d\le N}\mu(d)\Bigl\lfloor\frac Nd\Bigr\rfloor^2.$$
Write $\lfloor N/d\rfloor = N/d - \theta_d$ with $0 \le \theta_d < 1$; then $\lfloor N/d\rfloor^2 = N^2/d^2 + E_d$ with $|E_d| \le 2N/d$. So
$$C(N) = N^2\sum_{d\le N}\frac{\mu(d)}{d^2} + O\Bigl(N\sum_{d\le N}\frac1d\Bigr) = \frac{N^2}{\zeta(2)} + O(N\log N),$$
using $\sum_d\mu(d)/d^2 = 1/\zeta(2)$ and $\sum_{d>N}d^{-2} \le 1/N$. Dividing by $N^2$, the probability is $6/\pi^2 + O(\log N/N)$. For $N = 1000$ there are $608383$ coprime pairs, a proportion of $0.6084$, against $6/\pi^2 \approx 0.6079$.

blocks.body:
- "$1 + 2 + 3 + \cdots = -\tfrac{1}{12}$" is not a statement about the series, which diverges. What is true is that the continuation of $\sum n^{-s}$ from $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$ takes the value $-\tfrac{1}{12}$ at $s = -1$. A legitimate shadow of it: the smoothed sum $\sum_n n e^{-n/N}$ equals $N^2 - \tfrac{1}{12} + O(N^{-2})$, with constant term $\zeta(-1)$ (see [[functional-equation]]).
- The series and the Euler product are valid only for $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$. Nonvanishing "because of the Euler product" says nothing inside the critical strip.
- The formula $\zeta(-n) = -B_{n+1}/(n+1)$ is for $n \ge 1$; at $n = 0$ it depends on the sign convention for $B_1$.
- No closed form is known for $\zeta(3), \zeta(5), \dots$. Apéry proved in 1978 that $\zeta(3)$ is irrational; whether $\zeta(5)$ is irrational is unknown.
- $\zeta$ has a pole at $s = 1$ but is finite at every other point of the line $\operatorname{Re} s = 1$, and its nonvanishing there is a theorem (1896), not a triviality.

- [[functional-equation]]: Riemann's symmetry between $s$ and $1-s$, which completes the continuation, explains the trivial zeros and produces the values $\zeta(-n)$.
- [[pnt]]: Perron's formula ([[mellin]]) applied to $-\zeta'/\zeta$, together with $\zeta(1+it) \ne 0$, gives $\pi(x) \sim x/\log x$.
- [[l-functions]]: replacing $1$ by a Dirichlet character $\chi(n)$ gives $L(s,\chi)$, which detects primes in arithmetic progressions.
- [[dedekind-zeta]]: the zeta function of a number field; for $\mathbb Q(i)$ it factors as $\zeta(s)L(s,\chi_{-4})$, where $\chi_{-4}$ is the nontrivial character modulo 4.
- [[nontrivial-zeros]] and [[rh]]: counting and locating the zeros in the critical strip.

1. Use $B_8 = -\tfrac{1}{30}$ to show that $\zeta(8) = \pi^8/9450$.
2. Show that $\sum_{n\le N}\frac1n - \log N = 1 - \int_1^N\frac{\{x\}}{x^2}\,dx$, and deduce that $\gamma = \lim_{N\to\infty}\bigl(\sum_{n\le N}\frac1n - \log N\bigr)$.
3. Show that $(1 - 2^{1-s})\zeta(s) = \sum_{n\ge1}(-1)^{n-1}n^{-s}$ for $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$. The right side converges and is positive for real $s > 0$; use this to show that $\zeta(s) < 0$ for $0 < s < 1$.
4. Prove that $\zeta(\bar s) = \overline{\zeta(s)}$ wherever $\zeta$ is defined.
